The disciples asked about the end of the age in connection with the temple (Matthew 24:3). Jesus had just said the house would be left desolate and that "all these things will come upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36-38). So the "end" here is that end. On the fulfilled reading, "saved" includes being kept alive through the war, though it does not exclude final salvation. Jesus told them to flee to the mountains when they saw the sign (Matthew 24:16). Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella beyond the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Henry Alford wrote that no Christian is known to have died in the siege. The word "end" always needs its context. Here the context is the temple.
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3: believers in Jerusalem moved to Pella, a city of the Decapolis, before the siege.
Luke 21:18-19: "Not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives."

Many interpreters take "the end" as the end of a believer's life or the end of history, and "saved" as eternal salvation. Some scholars question how much of the Pella tradition is historical. Futurists see the verse as speaking to believers who live through the final tribulation.
If "the end" in Matthew 24 is still future, why do futurist timelines have so much happening after it?
Because "end" always means the end of something named in the context. This reading says the context of Matthew 24 is the end of the temple age.

Futurist timelines place many events after the "end": a great tribulation, Christ's return, a thousand-year kingdom, a final rebellion, and the new heavens and earth. So even on their view, the "end" of Matthew 24:14 is not the end of everything. On the fulfilled reading, this shows that "end" must be defined by its setting. In Matthew 24 the setting is the disciples' question about the temple and the end of the age (Matthew 24:2-3). The kingdom would be taken from the leaders of that time and given to a fruitful people (Matthew 21:43-45). For them it was "the end". Revelation likewise says its events are "near" (Revelation 1:3). Pushing these texts two thousand years away makes time words almost meaningless.
1 Peter 4:7: "The end of all things is at hand" was written to believers in the AD 60s.
1 Corinthians 15:24 speaks of a different "end": when Christ hands over the kingdom after defeating death.

Futurists answer that "the end" in Matthew 24 means the end of the present age before the kingdom, which fits their timeline. Amillennial readers see one final end at Christ's return. Many agree that the word needs context, but they read the context as wider than the temple.
Was the gospel preached "in the whole world" before AD 70, as Matthew 24:14 requires?
Yes, according to Paul. He wrote that the gospel had been proclaimed "in all creation under heaven" and was bearing fruit "in the whole world".

Jesus said, "This gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come" (Matthew 24:14). Some futurist writers stress that the end can come only after the gospel reaches all nations. On the fulfilled reading, Paul says this had happened in his own day. The gospel "has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven" (Colossians 1:23). It was "bearing fruit and growing in the whole world" (Colossians 1:6). The faith of the Romans was "proclaimed in all the world" (Romans 1:8). Paul applied Psalm 19:4 to the preaching: "Their voice has gone out to all the earth" (Romans 10:18). Henry Alford noted that every nation of the Roman world had heard before Jerusalem fell. That gave scattered Jewish communities a chance to receive Christ.
Acts 19:10: "All the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks", within two years.
Romans 15:24, 28: Paul planned to go to Spain, the western edge of the known world.

Futurists and many others say Paul used representative or hopeful language, and that Matthew 24:14 still drives world missions today. They connect it with Revelation 7:9, where people from every nation stand before the throne. Many amillennial readers see a first fulfillment then and a fuller one before the return.
What does "whole world" (oikoumene) mean in Matthew 24:14?
It means the inhabited world known to the writer, often the Roman Empire. Luke uses the same word for Caesar's census of "all the world".

The Greek word in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene, "the inhabited earth". Luke 2:1 uses the same word: Caesar Augustus ordered that "all the world" should be registered. That clearly means the Roman Empire. Agabus foretold a famine over "all the world" (oikoumene), which happened under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Paul's enemies said he stirred up Jews "throughout the world" (Acts 24:5). Some critics, such as Thomas Ice, ask whether preterists think the gospel reached the Western Hemisphere before AD 70. The fulfilled reading answers with the same question about Luke 2:1. No one thinks Augustus took a census of the Americas. Words must be read as their first readers used them. Even where kosmos is used, Paul says the gospel had gone into the whole world (Colossians 1:6).
Luke 2:1: "a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world (oikoumene) should be registered."
Acts 17:6: the missionaries were accused of turning "the world" (oikoumene) upside down.

Futurists accept that oikoumene can mean the Roman world. They argue that Matthew's "all nations" (also in Matthew 28:19) widens the scope to the whole globe. Some scholars note that oikoumene can also mean the whole inhabited earth in other texts (Acts 17:31).
Does "to all nations" in Matthew 24:14 mean every people group on earth today?
This reading says no. Paul wrote that the gospel "has been made known to all nations" in his day, using the same phrase.

Some commentators argue that "all nations" sets the scope of Matthew 24:14. Since not every nation had heard before AD 70, they say, the verse is still future. But Paul ends Romans by praising God for the gospel that "has now been disclosed and made known to all nations" (Romans 16:25-26). If "all nations" sets the scope, Paul says it was met. The parallel in Mark says the gospel must "first be proclaimed to all nations" (Mark 13:10), again in the context of the disciples' own trials. Philip Doddridge, an 18th-century writer, gathered early traditions that apostles preached in Syria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Parthia, Persia, India and the west within thirty years of the cross. Many of these traditions are late and uncertain. But Paul's own statement is clear.
Acts 2:5-11: at Pentecost there were Jews "from every nation under heaven", from Parthia to Rome, who heard the gospel and carried it home.
Acts 8:27-39: an Ethiopian court official believed and returned to Africa.

Many missions-minded Christians read Matthew 24:14 as an unfinished task that must be completed before Christ returns. They see Paul's words as a statement of the gospel's reach in principle, not a completed census. Others hold both: a first-century fulfillment and a continuing pattern for mission.
Do modern plans for a third temple in Jerusalem relate to Bible prophecy?
This reading says no. Some groups prepare vessels and priestly garments, but no New Testament verse links a future temple to God's plan.

Since the 1980s some Jewish groups have studied how to rebuild the temple and restore its priesthood. The Temple Institute in Jerusalem has made vessels and garments. Stories spread among Christians about stones cut abroad or a prefabricated temple. Some Christian writers see these plans as signs that the end is near. On the fulfilled reading, such plans have no role in the fulfillment of prophecy. The New Testament nowhere says a temple must be rebuilt. The temple Jesus spoke of was the one standing in his day, which fell in AD 70. Christians should treat their Jewish neighbours' hopes with respect. But they should not build their own theology on news reports. Many Jewish leaders themselves are divided, and some teach that the Messiah alone may rebuild.
A 1989 news report described a small group of Israelis and Jews abroad quietly preparing for a third temple.
Maimonides (12th century) taught that the Messiah would rebuild the temple (Mishneh Torah, Kings 11.1); many rabbis therefore oppose human efforts now.

Dispensational writers believe a third temple will be built, either before or during a future seven-year tribulation. They see current preparations as preparing the stage. Most amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial Christians agree with this reading that no rebuilt temple is required by Scripture.
What happened to predictions that the temple would be rebuilt by a certain date?
They failed. For example, a Jerusalem rabbi said in 1991 that the temple would be rebuilt in 1992. Dates like this show the danger of reading headlines as prophecy.

During the Gulf War of 1991 a Jerusalem-based rabbi linked the war with Iraq to old texts about Babylon. He said preparation for the Messiah began with the Balfour Declaration of 1917, continued with Jerusalem's reunification in 1967, and would end with the temple's rebuilding in 1992. That year passed with no temple. Christian writers have made similar forecasts. On the fulfilled reading, these failures repeat a pattern. Current events are tied to prophecy, dates are set, and then the dates pass. Jesus warned against being led astray by people who say "the time is at hand" (Luke 21:8). The safest path is to read prophecy in its own time setting and to test claims by Scripture rather than by the news.
Luke 21:8: Jesus warned of those who say "The time is at hand! Do not go after them."
Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) suggested the generation after 1948 would see the end within about forty years.

Futurist teachers today usually avoid dates and say only that a temple will be built at some point. They agree that failed predictions are harmful. They argue that failed dates show human error, not that the temple prophecies are false.
Does the New Testament predict that the temple will be rebuilt?
No verse says so. Even leading futurist writers admit there is no verse that says "there will be a third temple". They infer it from other texts.

Read the New Testament for a promise of a rebuilt temple, and none is found. Futurist authors Thomas Ice and Timothy Demy wrote that there are no Bible verses that say there will be a third temple. They infer it from texts that mention a temple in the end-time events: Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2. On the fulfilled reading, there is a simple reason for the silence. The real temple of God in the New Testament is the church, built on Christ as the cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4-7). The stone temple was about to pass away (Hebrews 8:13). The three texts that mention a temple were all written while Herod's temple still stood. Their first readers would have thought of that building.
Ephesians 2:20-22: believers are "being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit".
1 Corinthians 3:16: "Do you not know that you are God's temple?" Paul wrote this while the Jerusalem temple stood.

Futurists say a rebuilt temple is a valid inference, as the Trinity is a valid inference without the word. They argue that 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11 describe events that did not happen in AD 70, so a later temple is needed. Others read these texts as symbols of the church.
Why do futurist systems need a rebuilt temple?
Because they place the "abomination of desolation" and the man of lawlessness in the future. Those events need a temple standing in Jerusalem.

In the futurist scheme, a future Antichrist makes a covenant with Israel for seven years. In the middle he breaks it, stops the sacrifices and sets himself up in a rebuilt temple as God. This is the "abomination of desolation" (Matthew 24:15; Daniel 9:27) and the man of lawlessness sitting in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4). So a temple must exist for this to happen. On the fulfilled reading, the need for a rebuilt temple comes from the system, not from the texts. When Jesus spoke of "the holy place", the temple was still standing in "the holy city" (Matthew 4:5; 27:53). He walked away from that temple (Matthew 24:1). His disciples would have thought of it, not of a building to be raised two thousand years later.
Luke 21:20 explains the "abomination" for Gentile readers: "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near."
Matthew 4:5 and 27:53 call first-century Jerusalem "the holy city".

Dispensationalists answer that the rebuilt temple is required by a literal reading of Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2, which they say were not fulfilled in AD 70. Some non-dispensational futurists share this view. Others read the "temple" in 2 Thessalonians as the church.
Which temple did Jesus mean when he spoke of the abomination "standing in the holy place" (Matthew 24:15)?
On this reading, the temple standing at that time, the one the disciples had just pointed out. Nothing in the text points to a different building.

The setting of Matthew 24 is one temple. Jesus leaves it (24:1). The disciples point to its buildings. He says its stones will be thrown down (24:2). He then tells them what sign to watch for: "When you see the abomination of desolation... standing in the holy place, then let those in Judea flee to the mountains" (24:15-16). The command to flee from Judea only makes sense for people living there when the sign appears. Luke records the same moment as Jerusalem being surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). On the fulfilled reading, Jesus would not leave out a crucial detail such as a temple being rebuilt if one were needed. If a future building were meant, his hearers would have had no way to know it.
Josephus (Jewish War 6.6.1) records that Roman soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them after it burned.
Daniel 11:31 and 1 Maccabees 1:54 describe an earlier "abomination" under Antiochus IV in 167 BC, in the second temple.

Futurists answer that the abomination includes a person who claims to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4), which did not happen in AD 70. They see a future temple. Some amillennial and historic premillennial readers see AD 70 as a first fulfillment and expect a final, greater one.
What temple would the first readers of 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2 have thought of?
The one still standing in Jerusalem. This reading says all New Testament texts that mention the temple in prophecy were written before AD 70.

Futurist writers rely on three main New Testament texts for a future temple: Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1-2. Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians about AD 50-51, while the temple stood. On the fulfilled reading, Revelation was also written before AD 70, likely in the reign of Nero. In Revelation 11:1-2 John is told to measure the temple and altar but to leave out the outer court. It will be trampled by the nations for forty-two months. The Roman war against Judea lasted about that long, from spring AD 67 to August AD 70. Any reader in the 50s or 60s would have taken these words as referring to the existing temple. To look for another building, the reader would need a clear signal in the text.
Luke 21:24: "Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles", the same image as Revelation 11:2.
Vespasian began the campaign in Galilee in spring AD 67; the temple fell in August AD 70, about 42 months later.

Most scholars date Revelation to about AD 95, under Domitian, citing Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3). On that dating the temple in Revelation 11 must be symbolic (often the church) or future. Many amillennial scholars read 2 Thessalonians 2:4 as the church or as a general picture of blasphemy.
Is there a gap of two thousand years between the 69th and 70th weeks of Daniel 9?
This reading says no. Daniel presents seventy weeks as one unbroken period. Nothing in the text signals a pause after the 69th week.

Daniel 9:24 says "seventy weeks are decreed" to finish transgression, make atonement and bring everlasting righteousness. Verses 25-27 count seven weeks, then sixty-two weeks, then one week. Dispensationalists place the first 69 weeks before the Messiah's death. They then insert a gap of the church age before the last week, which they place in the future. On the fulfilled reading, this breaks the plain sense of a counted number. If someone said "seventy years" and stopped the clock after sixty-nine, the count would lose meaning. Jeremiah's seventy years ran without a break (Daniel 9:2). The text says the Messiah would "make a strong covenant with many for one week" and "put an end to sacrifice" in the middle (Daniel 9:27). This reading sees that in Christ's ministry and death, with the city's destruction following.
Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10: Daniel read Jeremiah's seventy years as a continuous span (Daniel 9:2).
Hebrews 10:9-10, 18: Christ's offering did away with the old sacrifices; "there is no longer any offering for sin."

Dispensationalists defend the gap by pointing to other prophecies with gaps, such as Isaiah 61:1-2 in Luke 4:18-19. They read "he" in Daniel 9:27 as "the prince who is to come", the Antichrist, not the Messiah. Many scholars also hold that the seventieth week ends with the events of AD 70 or with the gospel going to the Gentiles.
Is the gap in Daniel's seventy weeks a new idea in church history?
Its modern form, with a secret rapture and a church-age parenthesis, came in the 1800s. But some early writers also placed the last week at the end of history.

The fulfilled reading stresses that the dispensational "great parenthesis" became popular through J. N. Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). Most commentators before them, from Eusebius to the Reformers, saw the seventy weeks fulfilled in Christ's first coming. A correction is needed, however. Some early church writers did separate the last week. Irenaeus (about AD 180) placed half of the last week under the Antichrist (Against Heresies 5.25.4). Hippolytus (about AD 204) explicitly put the seventieth week at the end of the world (Commentary on Daniel 4.35; On Christ and Antichrist 43). So a gap is not entirely new. What is new is the full system built on it. The strongest case for this reading rests on the text of Daniel, not on history alone.
Eusebius (Demonstration of the Gospel 8.2) tied the seventy weeks to Christ's coming and the following events in Judea.
The Scofield Reference Bible's note on Daniel 9:24 spread the parenthesis view widely in the 20th century.

Dispensationalists cite Irenaeus and Hippolytus to show that a future seventieth week has early roots. Others note that many church fathers held a variety of views on Daniel 9. Historians agree that the full pretribulational system with a church-age parenthesis was formed in the 1830s.
What is God's temple in the New Testament?
Christ himself, and the people joined to him. Believers are "living stones" built into a spiritual house where God's Spirit lives.

Peter writes, "You yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says believers "are the temple of the living God" (2 Corinthians 6:16). He describes Jews and Gentiles joined on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. In him the whole structure grows into "a holy temple in the Lord" (Ephesians 2:20-22). Each believer's body is also a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). On the covenantal reading, this is the temple that the prophets' hopes pointed to. It is made of people from every nation. It is not torn down by armies. Calling for a new stone temple, on this view, turns attention back from the reality to the shadow.
1 Corinthians 3:16-17: "God's temple is holy, and you are that temple."
Revelation 21:22: in the new Jerusalem John saw no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb".

All Christian traditions agree that the church is now God's temple. Dispensationalists hold this too but add that God will also restore a physical temple for Israel's role in the tribulation and millennium. They see the church and a future temple as serving different purposes in God's plan.
Were the Old Testament promises of a rebuilt temple fulfilled?
Yes, on this reading. They were fulfilled when the exiles rebuilt the temple after Babylon and, more fully, in Christ and his church.

Prophets such as Haggai and Zechariah urged the returned exiles to rebuild the temple. It was finished in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15). Haggai promised that the glory of the latter house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). This reading says that greater glory came when the Lord himself entered that temple in the person of Jesus (Malachi 3:1). Zechariah said a man named "the Branch" would build the temple of the LORD and be a priest on his throne (Zechariah 6:12-13). The New Testament presents Jesus as that priest-king building a house of living stones (Hebrews 3:3-6). Amos foretold the rebuilding of "the booth of David". James said this was being fulfilled as Gentiles turned to God (Acts 15:15-17).
Ezra 6:15: the second temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius, 516 BC.
Acts 15:16-17: James quotes Amos 9:11-12 about rebuilding David's fallen tent and applies it to the Gentile mission.

Dispensationalists agree some promises were fulfilled after the exile. They argue that others, such as Ezekiel 40-48 and Zechariah 14, describe a future millennial temple, because their details did not fit the second temple. Some progressive dispensationalists accept the Acts 15 reading as an initial fulfillment.
How should Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezekiel 40-48) be read?
This reading sees it as a vision for the exiles about restored worship, written in the symbols of their day, and fulfilled at last in Christ and his church.

Ezekiel received the vision in 573 BC, during the exile (Ezekiel 40:1). E. W. Hengstenberg argued that its first readers would have expected it to apply to the return from Babylon. Jeremiah had promised the city and temple would be restored after seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10). Ezekiel himself said restoration would follow soon after destruction (Ezekiel 11:16-17). On this reading, the vision gave the exiles a picture of a purified people, with God dwelling among them. The river flowing from the temple to heal the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:1-12) is clearly symbolic, and Jesus used the image for the Spirit (John 7:37-39). Revelation 21-22 then takes up Ezekiel's images for the new Jerusalem. The vision points beyond any building to God's presence with his people.
Ezekiel 48:35: the city's name will be "The LORD is there". Revelation 21:3 says God's dwelling is with people.
Ezekiel 47:12 and Revelation 22:2 both describe trees by the river whose leaves bring healing.

Dispensationalists read Ezekiel 40-48 as a literal temple in a future millennium, because of its detailed measurements. Many amillennial scholars read it as symbolic of the church or the new creation. Some see it as an ideal plan that the post-exilic community never fully carried out.
Do some futurist writers teach that two more temples are coming?
Yes. Some teach a third temple to be defiled by the Antichrist and a fourth, millennial temple described by Ezekiel. This reading finds neither in the New Testament.

Some popular writers describe four temples in all. The first was Solomon's. The second was rebuilt after the exile and expanded by Herod. A third will be built on Mount Moriah and desecrated by the Antichrist. A fourth will be built in the millennium by the Messiah, following Ezekiel 40-48. On the fulfilled reading, this multiplies buildings that the New Testament never mentions. Hebrews, which explains the temple more than any other book, says nothing of a future rebuilding or of a millennial temple. It says instead that the first covenant is obsolete and ready to vanish (Hebrews 8:13). It says believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). The only future temple the New Testament describes is God and the Lamb (Revelation 21:22).
Hebrews 9:8-9: the first tent was "a symbol for the present age" while it was still standing.
Hebrews 12:22: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."

Dispensationalists hold that the third and fourth temples follow from a literal reading of Daniel 9:27, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Ezekiel 40-48. They see no conflict with Hebrews, since Hebrews addresses the church, not Israel in the millennium. Many other Christians find this distinction unconvincing.
Would animal sacrifices in a future millennial temple conflict with the book of Hebrews?
This reading says yes. Ezekiel's sacrifices are "to make atonement", while Hebrews says Christ's one offering ended all offerings for sin.

Ezekiel 45:15, 17 and 20 describe offerings "to make atonement" for the people and the house. The same word is used in the law of Moses for sacrifices that cover sin (Leviticus 16:30-34). Hebrews teaches that the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Hebrews 10:12). Where there is forgiveness, "there is no longer any offering for sin" (Hebrews 10:18). On the fulfilled reading, a future temple with atoning sacrifices would have Jesus overseeing the very offerings his blood replaced. That seems to go against the whole message of Hebrews. This reading therefore takes Ezekiel's vision as describing worship for the restored community after the exile, in the forms they knew.
Hebrews 10:1: the law has only "a shadow of the good things to come", not the true form.
Ezekiel 43:18-27 describes a seven-day sin offering to cleanse the altar, using the language of atonement.

Dispensational scholars such as Jerry Hullinger argue that Ezekiel's sacrifices remove ritual uncleanness so God can dwell among a still-mortal people. They say this does not deal with eternal guilt, which Christ alone removes. Others see the sacrifices as memorials, like the Lord's Supper.
Can the sacrifices in Ezekiel's temple be explained as memorials?
This reading finds that hard. The text calls them offerings "to make atonement", not memorials. Calling them memorials departs from the literal reading the system requires.

The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) offered two options for Ezekiel's sacrifices. Either they will be memorials looking back to the cross, or the reference to sacrifices is not literal. On the fulfilled reading, both options create a problem. Nothing in Ezekiel says the sacrifices are memorials. They are offerings for atonement (Ezekiel 45:15, 17). The second option gives up literal reading, which dispensationalism names as its key rule. Charles Ryrie defined literal interpretation as giving each word its normal meaning. By that rule, atonement means atonement. This reading concludes that it is simpler to read Ezekiel as speaking to the restored exiles in their own terms. The vision should not be moved 2,500 years ahead into a kingdom where atoning blood is offered in the presence of the crucified Christ.
The Lord's Supper is a true memorial: "Do this in remembrance of me" (1 Corinthians 11:24-25), but it uses bread and cup, not blood sacrifice.
Ezekiel 45:17: the prince provides offerings "to make atonement for the house of Israel".

Many dispensationalists now prefer the view that the sacrifices bring ritual cleansing, not memorials. They note that Old Testament sacrifices also never removed sin in an ultimate sense (Hebrews 10:4), yet God commanded them. On that view, millennial offerings could serve a similar temporary purpose without denying the cross.
Was the earthly temple designed to become obsolete?
On this reading, yes. God said heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so no house can contain him. The temple was a copy that would give way to Christ.

Isaiah 66:1 says, "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?" Solomon said the same at the temple's dedication: heaven itself cannot contain God, "how much less this house" (1 Kings 8:27). The tabernacle was made after a pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40). Hebrews explains that it was a copy of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 8:5; 9:24). On the covenantal reading, the temple was built with an end in view. Jesus' body was the lasting temple (John 2:19-21). He said worship would no longer be bound to Jerusalem (John 4:21-24). Paul says the present Jerusalem is in slavery with her children, while the Jerusalem above is free (Galatians 4:25-26).
Acts 7:48-50: Stephen quoted Isaiah 66:1-2 before the council, shortly before he was stoned.
Hebrews 9:24: Christ entered "not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself".

Most Christians agree the temple pointed to Christ. Dispensationalists argue that a temple's role as a type does not prevent God from using a literal temple again in the future. They note that God told David's son to build it and promised blessing for the house (2 Samuel 7:13).
Why does Isaiah 66:3 compare offering an ox to killing a man?
Because worship without a humble heart is worthless to God. This reading applies the verse especially to sacrifice offered after Christ's one true sacrifice.

Isaiah 66:3 says that whoever slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man, and whoever offers grain is like one who offers pig's blood. God says this of those who have "chosen their own ways". In verse 2 he says he looks to the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word. The prophets often said God rejects ritual without obedience (Isaiah 1:11-15; Amos 5:21-24). Edward J. Young applied Isaiah 66:3 first to those who built the second temple in their own spirit, and more fully to those who kept offering sacrifices after Christ's one sacrifice. On this reading, once the true Lamb had come, the old sacrifices could no longer be offered as before. This reading stresses that this is a theological claim about sacrifices, not a judgment on the hearts of Jewish people in general.
